findings.statement: AstraZeneca completed a 'Harmonised Listing Structure' effective after market close on 30 January 2026: it voluntarily withdrew its ADSs (representing ordinary shares on a two-for-one basis) and its US debt securities from Nasdaq, and its ordinary shares and debt securities began trading on the NYSE from Monday, 2 February 2026, retaining the ticker symbol AZN.

Following the harmonisation, AstraZeneca ordinary shares are tradeable across three venues: the London Stock Exchange (primary listing, LSE), Nasdaq Stockholm, and now the New York Stock Exchange (direct listing of ordinary shares rather than ADSs), giving investors a single global security fungible across exchanges.

A Form 8-A12B filed 22 January 2026 registered transfer of 20 series of US dollar-denominated debt securities issued by AstraZeneca PLC and AstraZeneca Finance LLC from Nasdaq to the NYSE, consistent with the harmonisation of listing venues for both equity and debt.

Shareholders now hold and vote interests via different registries depending on venue: direct NYSE ordinary shareholders, the AstraZeneca Corporate Sponsored Nominee (CSN), Nasdaq Stockholm shareholders, and UK Depositary Interest (UK DI) holders, each with separate voting/registrar arrangements (Computershare UK, Sweden, and US entities) — indicating a fragmented but harmonised multi-venue shareholder base post-listing restructuring.

AstraZeneca's Notice of AGM 2026 (filed as 6-K, 10 March 2026) explicitly references 'the completion of the Company's listing harmonisation earlier this year' as materially affecting shareholder voting mechanics, corroborating that the harmonised structure was fully operative by early 2026.

Press materials (not citable as evidence, only as web listings) indicate the harmonisation was first announced 29 September 2025 amid broader industry commentary about pharma companies reconsidering UK listings, and framed by AstraZeneca as intended to 'deliver a global listing for global investors in a global company.'

On consistency: a 2.5% perpetuity at ~8% WACC implies a materially higher terminal multiple than 11.5x, so the two are not identical; I regard the perpetuity-growth figure as the better estimate of terminal value, with 11.5x a deliberately conservative cross-check. assumptions.name: terminal_growth
assumptions.justification: Taken as below an ordinary WACC of roughly 8-9% for AZN (5.11% derived risk-free plus a modest equity premium on a low-beta, investment-grade pharma). 2.5% sits near long-run nominal global GDP and is above pure inflation only because the portfolio is geographically diversified with emerging-market exposure. It is not the trailing 11.9% CAGR: that reflects the Alexion consolidation and current launches, not perpetuity, and early-2030s LOEs on Tagrisso/Farxiga/Imfinzi argue against extrapolating it. Evidence of pipeline replenishment (tozorakimab, efzimfotase, I-CAN, CSPC/Jacobio deals) supports growth at, not below, nominal GDP. Lower it toward 1.5-2% if you judge patent-cliff replacement incomplete; raise it only if the risk-free rate is read as signalling durably higher nominal growth.
